_comment: Date-free prose for /measured and /measured.md. Band ids match measured.json.
whyHtml:
The browser can’t paint text until a few things arrive, often one after another: the HTML; the stylesheet for that text, unless the CSS is inlined in the HTML; and, if the font loads with font-display: block, the font file. Each can depend on the one before it. This is the critical request chain, and every link in it costs a full round trip.

Under mobile Lighthouse (simulated Slow 4G and a 4× CPU slowdown), each round trip costs about 0.4–0.6 s, and they all cost about the same. Making a request smaller barely moves FCP. Removing it saves a whole step. A cache is either warm or cold, so it adds a step or it doesn’t.

That is why results bunch into bands instead of spreading out, and why a partial fix doesn’t move an app part of the way. Inlining the CSS while keeping a blocking font request leaves the app in the same band. It moves only when a whole link leaves the chain.

bands.fast:
The first response holds everything needed to paint. The CSS is inlined in a <style> tag, the font is self-hosted and preloaded (or text paints in a fallback font while it loads), and the server sends the HTML without waiting on a slow database query.

Any app whose first paint needs only the HTML lands here, whatever the framework.
bands.middle:
The HTML arrives, then the browser waits for one more round of requests before it paints. Usually that is a stylesheet linked from the HTML: the app’s own CSS bundle, a Google Fonts stylesheet, or both fetched side by side. A self-hosted font that isn’t preloaded, or a server render that misses the cache, adds the same single step.

This is where most frameworks’ default settings put the Books app: the CSS ships as a separate file, so the browser can’t paint until it arrives.
bands.slow-middle:
Two requests wait in sequence after the HTML, or the HTML itself is slow because a cache or a serverless worker was cold. A cold worker has to start, query the database and render before it sends the first byte. The same code can measure a band faster a few minutes later, once the cache is warm.

The fix is usually in caching and deployment, not in the components: keep the HTML cached at the edge and make the data cache persistent.
bands.baseline:
The full waterfall:

HTML (waits on a database query)
  -> render-blocking CSS bundle
    -> Google Fonts CSS from fonts.googleapis.com
      -> woff2 from fonts.gstatic.com (display=block)

That is four requests in sequence, two of them to new origins. Preconnecting to the Google origins saves the DNS and TLS setup, but both requests still have to finish before text paints, because display=block hides text until the font arrives.

earlierHtml:
An earlier round of measurements covered six ports whose naive builds used the full waterfall above: a linked CSS bundle and the Geist font loaded from Google Fonts. Every one of them landed in Baseline. Their optimized builds at that point had dropped Google Fonts but still kept one or two links in the chain, so they stopped around Middle instead of reaching Fast.

None of the current naive builds is that slow, so this is the only place on the site where the Baseline band is filled.
earlierNoteHtml: These are older builds than the chart above, and each figure is the average of single Lighthouse runs on Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare, not a median of repeated runs. Read the two charts separately.
tieHtml: A band is a tie. Lighthouse doesn’t slow the real load down. It loads the page at full speed and estimates what Slow 4G would do from that trace, so the tenths of a second between ports in one band come from the estimate, not from the app. Angular is the clearest case: both its builds land under 0.9 s, ahead of every other port, yet in the real load other Fast ports paint as soon or sooner. The estimate likely favours Angular because its first response has fewer requests that look critical: the CSS and the Google Fonts stylesheet are inlined. Benchmark shows the real load’s first paint as Raw FCP next to the estimate.
